The SS_ID advances by one per FEC source packet, modulo 2^32, in the order the publisher emits the packets ( Section C.5.2), and the blocks of an FEC instance are consecutive: each starts at the SS_ID that follows the last source symbol of its predecessor ( Section 5.4). Every transport path yields the same SS_ID for the same packet, because each path carries the same MMTP packet, so receivers MAY combine symbols from any transport path toward the same FEC block recovery. A loc or cmaf track reaches multicast only through a separate mmtp rendition track ( Section 4.1), whose symbols belong to another FEC instance.

OTI and sub-blocks: MoQ carries no RaptorQ Object Transmission Information (OTI, Section 3.3) in-session: receivers derive it per block from the instance's configuration and the block's SSB_length per Section 6.1. The AL-FEC message of an MMTP session (Section 8.3) carries none either. When a source block is too large to decode in the decoder's working memory, RFC 6330 permits dividing each block into N sub-blocks (the Number of Sub-Blocks field of the OTI). The derived OTI fixes N = 1, so catalog-signaled sessions do not use sub-blocks; the AL-FEC message of carries no OTI, and the split source blocks of its Clause C.2.2 are the two-stage coding structure, which this profile does not use. A publisher using MMTP packaging under this profile therefore uses ssbg_mode1 without sub-blocks, and never ssbg_mode2.

section.name: Source FEC Payload ID
section.t: Exactly one 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID (SS_ID; ffsrpts_flag = 0, so no FFSRP_TS, Section C.5.1) is appended at the end of each MMTP FEC source packet -- following the MMTP payload, outside the MMTP packet header -- with or without a keyframe overlay (). The trailer lies outside the declared MPU payload (Section 5.2) and outside the protected packet ().

For MoQ-only receivers (no A3SA verification), the trailing 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID remains the canonical identifier by which a source packet is placed in its block ( Section 5.5). QUIC transport encryption provides equivalent integrity protection. states why the ATSC 3.0 signing mechanism does not authenticate the trailer, and what a receiver that requires authenticated block assignment does instead.

Whatever the receiver's verification posture, the FEC Source Info Object Property ( Section 5.6) carries the same value for a receiver that does not parse the packet; where an object delivers both and they disagree, the trailer is the one that is canonical, because it is the field the FEC encoder emitted and the one the receiver locates the symbol by. The Property restates it at the MoQ layer.

On an mmtp source object the Property's value is the 4-byte form of Section 5.6, which names instance 0: the sequence number of the source symbol the object carries, the same value and the same definition that the Source FEC Payload ID trailer of the FEC source packet carries. The Property is that trailer's MoQ-layer carrier: one identifier, one definition, whichever path the symbol travels. Both carry the same value and a publisher MUST make them identical, on every source object, because the object payload is the whole FEC source packet, trailer included. The Property is wanted there as well: it places the symbol at the MoQ layer, reachable by a relay and by a receiver that does not parse MMTP, whereas the trailer is the field the FEC encoder emitted. A packet the decoder recovers carries neither (): the Property is not recovered with the object, and the trailer is appended after FEC encoding, so a receiver that recovers a packet determines its SS_ID from the block coordinate that recovered it, within that FEC instance's SS_ID space; an overlay coordinate does not yield a base SS_ID.

Where a keyframe overlay applies (), an object carrying a Random Access Point fragment is a source symbol of two FEC instances, whose SS_ID spaces are disjoint, so "the source symbol the object carries" names two SS_IDs rather than one. The Property carries the base instance's SS_ID -- the value the Source FEC Payload ID trailer carries -- and a publisher MUST NOT place an overlay SS_ID in it. No second Property entry conveys the overlay SS_ID: it travels in the 0x8B01 MMTP header extension, which lies inside the MMTP packet header and is therefore part of the protected packet of both instances (), so it rides inside the object's payload on this path as on any other. A receiver takes an overlay SS_ID from that extension and from nothing else, and in particular MUST NOT infer one from the Property.

An object that carries a source symbol but no FEC Source Info Property violates the publisher requirement of Section 5.6. A receiver that does not parse the FEC source packet has no SS_ID for it -- at the MoQ layer the Property is the only carrier -- so it MUST NOT feed such an object to the base decoder and MUST NOT count it in K or in any base block, and MAY still deliver it as media. A receiver that parses the packet MAY take the SS_ID from the trailer instead, since the packaging delivers it; this is a deviation from that section, which has no trailer to fall back on. An overlay SS_ID is unaffected either way: it travels in the 0x8B01 MMTP header extension (), which the Property does not carry, and that section alone governs when the overlay decoder may be fed.

section.name: Repair Packet
section.t: Each object on a repair track is one complete MMTP repair packet (packet type 0x03, FEC Type 2) carrying exactly one repair symbol. Its layout is the ISO 23008-1 AL-FEC repair packet form -- the MMTP packet header followed by the 13-byte Repair FEC Payload ID and the repair symbol data ( Sections C.4.3 and C.5.3; ssbg_mode1, one-stage FEC with N = 1, and ffsrpts_flag = 0, so no FFSRP_TS, Section C.5.1) -- so the same repair packet is valid on MoQ, multicast UDP, and native broadcast paths without translation, and matches the repair-object depiction of . The layout below reproduces Section C.5.3 for convenience. The Repair FEC Payload ID carries the fields of the repair object of Section 7.5 with the semantics that section gives them -- SS_Start, RSB_length, RS_ID and SSB_length -- and this section defines only the MMTP packet header in front of them:

MMTP Packet Header: The standard 12-byte MMTP packet header (Section 3.1) with packet type 0x03 (repair) and FEC Type 2; its packet_id routes the repair flow. Like every packet of its MMTP packet flow, source and signaling packets included, a repair packet has the packet counter flag C = 0 (Section 3.1; Clause 9.2.3). A repair packet MUST NOT carry a header extension (X = 0). Because C = 0 and X = 0, the Repair FEC Payload ID always begins at byte offset 12.

A repair object under this profile is therefore 12 + 13 + T bytes long, not the 13 + T bytes that Section 7.5 requires of a repair object under "moq-object-v1"; a receiver MUST discard a repair object of an mmtp track whose payload is not exactly 12 + 13 + T bytes. It reads the Repair FEC Payload ID at byte offset 12, and every other rule of that section applies to the fields: a receiver routes the packet to the decoder of the instance that the configuration relates to the repair track it arrived on, and discards a packet whose RS_ID is not less than RSB_length or that fails a bound of the instance's scheme ( Section 7).

section.name: Keyframe Overlay
section.t: A source track MAY additionally be protected by a keyframe overlay: a second, independent FEC instance whose source symbols are only the fragments of Random Access Points of that source track. It is this profile's form of an overlapping instance ( Section 8.4). The overlay is defined only for a source track under "iso-ssbg1-v1", because its membership and its overlay SS_ID rely on the MMTP RAP_flag and header extension ( and ), which a loc or cmaf object does not have; a track under "moq-object-v1" has no overlay, and a catalog that declares one for such a track fails the rule of .

Losing part of a Random Access Point makes every dependent frame undecodable until the next one; the overlay protects RAP fragments across a block of its own, which can be wider than the base window, without changing the base instance's latency.

section.name: Overlay Instance
section.t: An overlay is a separate FEC instance over the same source track. It has its own sourceSymbols (K_overlay) and its own repairSymbols, declared on its own instance entry with its own repair track ( Section 3.1), and it shares the source track's scheme, blockProfile and symbolSize. It does not share the base instance's K, its block partition, its SS_ID space, or its RS_ID space. Because each source packet carries one base SS_ID, a different K or interleave window needs a separate rendition; the keyframe overlay is a separate FEC instance, not a layer.

The overlay's instance object carries one member that this document defines, under the rule of Section 3.4 that lets a block profile's document define further keys for the tracks it admits, and further exceptions among them:

scope (string, OPTIONAL): When present, MUST be "keyframe", and declares this instance to be the source track's keyframe overlay. It is an unknown-key exception (). An overlay is defined only for a source track under "iso-ssbg1-v1" ().

Every per-block quantity of -- K, the total repair count P, SS_ID, ESI, RS_ID, SS_Start, RSB_length, SSB_length, the short-block rules, the wrap epoch and repair group IDs, and the bounds of its Section 10.3 -- is defined within one FEC instance (its Section 5.1). For the base instance, K is the source track's sourceSymbols and P is the sum of repairSymbols over its published layers ( Section 7.3.1); for an overlay, K and P are the sourceSymbols and repairSymbols of its own instance. A repair packet belongs to the instance of the track it arrived on ().

An overlay is not a repair layer. It carries no repairLayer, it is not a member of the layer index chain, and it is excluded from the contiguity and priority monotonicity rules of Section 10.3, which order the base layer chain only. Its priority is independent within 192 to 255 ( Section 10.3, rule 10, and Section 11), and MAY be numerically lower than a base enhancement layer's so that a keyframe repair symbol is delivered before an ordinary one.

Overlay ESIs never collide with base ESIs because the two are different instances decoded by different decoders; a receiver does not feed a repair symbol of one instance to the decoder of the other, nor reuse a source symbol's coordinate in one instance as its coordinate in the other ( Section 5.1). A RAP source packet is a source symbol of both instances, at an unrelated coordinate in each ().

A source track has at most one overlay, a wire constraint explained in , and none when its blockProfile is "moq-object-v1"; the overlay instance's repair track carries no repairLayer. A receiver MUST validate this before starting FEC for an overlay instance of the source track, and on any violation MUST fail closed as Section 10.3 requires for its own rules: it reports the offending catalog path, does not start FEC for any overlay instance of that source track, and MUST NOT repair the catalog by ignoring a track. An overlay is declared only by the catalog, never in an in-band AL-FEC message, and only where no FEC source or repair packet carries FFSRP_TS ().

Under "reed-solomon" the overlay has its own bound: K_overlay + P_overlay is at most 255 ( Section 7), whatever the base instance uses, and its rows and columns of A are numbered within the overlay instance ( Section 5.2). An overlay with K_overlay 256 and P_overlay 32 has an RS_ID range of 0 to 31, an ESI range in a full overlay block of 256 to 287, and packets carrying RSB_length 32; it is valid only under "raptorq", since 256 + 32 = 288 exceeds 255. Under "reed-solomon", an overlay whose instance declares sourceSymbols 192 and repairSymbols 32 is valid, since 192 + 32 = 224.

section.name: Overlay Membership
section.t: The overlay's source symbols are the fragments of the source track that belong to a Random Access Point, in transmission order. A publisher that declares an overlay MUST set RAP_flag on a source packet of the track, MUST include the packet in the overlay instance, and MUST carry the packet's overlay SS_ID in its 0x8B01 header extension (), if and only if that packet's payload belongs to a keyframe MFU covered by the overlay.

Overlay source symbols are numbered consecutively within the overlay instance, in the order the publisher emits them: the overlay SS_ID is 0 at the first overlay source symbol of the stream and advances by one per overlay source symbol, modulo 2^32 ( Section 7.6). It is the value the RAP source packet carries in its 0x8B01 header extension (). It lives in the overlay instance's own SS_ID space, independent of the base instance's, and the two IDs on one packet are unrelated numbers. An overlay source block holds at most K_overlay overlay source symbols, and overlay blocks, including short ones, are formed, located and wrapped exactly as base blocks are ( Sections 5.4, 5.5 and 7.6), with K_overlay as the upper bound on their SSB_length. Because a RAP is a small fraction of the media, an overlay block spans many base blocks; the overlay's recovery latency is therefore its own block span and is unrelated to interleaveDepthMs.

A receiver knows that a source packet is an overlay source symbol because the packet carries the 0x8B01 header extension (). It knows that a repair packet belongs to the overlay because it arrives on the repair track that the catalog declares for the overlay instance of this source track, and that track has its own packet_id. The instance is therefore fixed by the track the packet arrived on; no field of the repair packet distinguishes the two, and a receiver does not infer the instance from SS_Start, RSB_length, or SSB_length, whose values are only interpretable once the instance is known ( Section 7.5).

section.name: Overlay SS_ID Header Extension
section.t: When the catalog declares a keyframe overlay for a source track (), a source packet of that track carrying a Random Access Point fragment is a source symbol of two FEC instances. It carries its base SS_ID in the one Source FEC Payload ID trailer that every FEC source packet carries (), and its overlay SS_ID () in an MMTP header extension ( Clause 9.2.3) of type 0x8B01:

A publisher that declares an overlay MUST carry this extension as the header extension, with X = 1, of exactly the source packets that it includes in the overlay instance, that is the packets on which it sets RAP_flag (), and of no other packet of the track. An MMTP packet carries at most one header extension ( Clause 9.2.3), so the RAP packets of a track under an overlay carry no other MMTP header extension, and a publisher that needs another header extension on those packets cannot use the overlay for that track. specifies no particular header extension and no registry of header extension types; this document uses the type 0x8B01 for the overlay SS_ID ().

The trailer is never more than one Source FEC Payload ID. On a packet with or without the extension, the last four bytes are the base SS_ID, as Section C.4.2 places it, so a receiver that does not implement overlays locates the trailer and the payload as on any other packet, stepping over the extension by its Length field. The extension lies inside the MMTP packet header, so it is part of the protected packet of both instances (), which protect one identical source symbol. The permission of Clause 9.2.3 to discard a header extension therefore extends only to a receiver's own processing: a node that forwards the packet MUST NOT remove or alter the extension. A RAP packet recovered by either instance carries its overlay SS_ID, so a receiver MAY place a RAP packet that the base instance recovered into the overlay block that the extension locates; states why the converse requires the packet's base SS_ID.

A receiver that implements overlays takes a packet's overlay SS_ID from this extension and from nothing else. It MUST NOT feed the overlay decoder a source packet that lacks the extension, whatever its RAP_flag, or one whose extension has a Length other than 4, and MUST NOT infer an overlay SS_ID from RAP_flag, from the packet's position, or from its base SS_ID.

A source track has at most one overlay () because a source packet has one header extension, and so carries one overlay SS_ID; relaxing that bound would be a revision of this document and a change to the source packet layout, not a catalog-only change.

The overlay is declared only by the catalog: Section 8.3 forbids describing the overlay's repair flow in an AL-FEC message, which identifies an FEC source flow by packet_id ( Clause C.6.3) and cannot describe the RAP subset that the overlay protects, so a receiver that consumes the flow without the catalog uses the base instance alone. An overlay is defined only without FFSRP_TS: a publisher MUST NOT declare an overlay for a source track whose FEC source or repair packets carry FFSRP_TS (ffsrpts_flag = 1, Section C.5.1), and the extension carries an SS_ID alone.
applies to the overlay SS_ID as to the base one: A3SA signing authenticates neither, and a receiver that requires authenticated block assignment treats each as that section requires.

section.name: Receiver Behavior
section.t: A receiver that implements overlays and has joined the overlay repair track decodes the two instances independently and MAY use the recovered RAP fragments even when the base instance failed to recover the block that carried them.

The overlay is the publisher-side half of keyframe protection. The receiver-side half is the repair policy of Section 6, under which a receiver gives a keyframe-bearing base block that in-band decoding leaves unrecovered priority unicast repair; its Section 6.6 states how the two combine.

A receiver that does not implement overlays MUST fail closed on a catalog that declares one for a track it intends to consume, that is on an FEC instance carrying the unknown scope key, and MUST NOT ignore the key and consume the source track anyway. This is an unknown-key exception that this document defines () under Section 3.4, which lets a block profile's document define further exceptions: a receiver that ignored the key could not tell the overlay's repair track from a repair layer of the base instance, and would feed the base decoder repair symbols of another FEC instance ().

This mechanism is not backward compatible with receivers that predate it, for the same reason. A publisher that must serve such receivers publishes the overlay on a separate source track, or does not publish it.

section.name: Interleaving
section.t: Interleaving and typical interleave windows (interleaveDepthMs) follow Section 9.3. A positive interleaveDepthMs is the elapsed source/repair send-span bound for each actual FEC block; it does not select FEC block boundaries, derive a number of groups per block, or require a fixed relationship between an FEC block and a media Group. A typical window for ARIB STD-B60 content is 2000 ms. The receiver's block-abandonment timeout -- how long it waits for a block's source and repair symbols before declaring the block unrecoverable -- follows the ISO receiver-buffer model Section 11.2.

Section 10.1 admits a positive interleaveDepthMs and lets a block profile give the value zero a meaning of its own. Under this profile the field MAY also be zero. A value of zero has the ISO meaning of using protection_window_size instead of a time window ( Clause C.6.3); this catalog profile carries no packet-count window. A catalog-only receiver therefore MUST NOT treat zero as a zero-duration span or use it to derive a block count, and has no elapsed-time FEC deadline from this field. If an applicable ISO packet-count window is accepted in-band, it governs separate count-based processing; it does not supply a millisecond deadline, it is not converted to milliseconds without an independently defined time mapping, and the receiver MUST NOT assume a media cadence to convert it. A publisher uses a zero value only with that ISO protection_window_size alternative. An absent field supplies no catalog-signaled span; neither an absent nor a zero value supplies an elapsed-time deadline. Without an elapsed-time deadline, open-block state is bounded only by the local policy of Section 9.4, and on a multicast or AMT leg the receiver performs no block classification or unicast repair ( Section 6) and keeps its repair-layer selection fixed (its Section 4).

section.name: FEC Parameter Signaling
section.t: FEC parameters for mmtp-packaged tracks are signaled in the catalog fec field, whose encoding defines (its Section 3) for the configuration data model of Section 10, which is authoritative for MoQ receivers (that section). A MoQ receiver requires no in-session FEC signaling: the catalog carries every FEC parameter it needs. This document does not redefine the catalog fields but specifies MMT-specific considerations for their use.

A publisher MAY also carry the MMTP AL-FEC signaling message of Section 8.3 on a MoQ mmtp source track, as an object whose payload is an MMTP signaling packet on packet_id 0 (Section 3.1). When present, it is published in Subgroup 0 of an MPU group as the object immediately before, and in the same subgroup as, that group's FT=0 object, and a group carries at most one such object (Sections 4.2 and 4.3). On a MoQ track such an object is a redundant in-band copy of catalog state: the message MUST NOT signal FEC parameters that contradict the track's catalog fec instances, and where the two disagree the catalog governs, as Section 10 requires of any in-band signaling. The object carries no media data unit and no repair symbol, so a MoQ receiver MUST NOT deliver it to a media or repair decoder (Section 3.1); a receiver that does not process MMTP signaling discards it.

The signaling object is not an FEC source symbol. Its MMTP packet has FEC Type 0 and no Source FEC Payload ID; it is not protected by any repair symbol, is not counted in any FEC block or in sourceSymbols (K), and has no SS_ID and no Encoding Symbol ID. Because it occupies an Object ID (Object ID 0 of its group, Section 4.6), Object IDs on an mmtp source track are not positions in the FEC block: a receiver MUST take each source symbol's SS_ID from the Source FEC Payload ID that trails its FEC Type 1 packet (), never from its Object ID, and places the symbol in its block by that SS_ID ( Section 5.5).

A MoQ track carries only the signaling packets its publisher chose to place on that track, so the packet_sequence_number values it exhibits on packet_id 0 need not be contiguous. A receiver MUST NOT infer loss from a packet_sequence_number gap on packet_id 0 of a MoQ track, and MUST NOT defer any packet, including a later packet on packet_id 0, behind such a gap.

section.t: When used with MMT packaging, the instance parameters of Section 10.1, as the catalog encodes them ( Section 3.1), map as follows:

When ingesting broadcast content, use the ISO protection-window signaling or a known source/repair send-span bound. A source-frame count alone does not bound the actual packet send span.

Signal the keyframe cadence in keyframeIntervalMs (or keyframeIntervalTicks), and the frame rate in the framerate field (Sections 4.4.2, 4.4.3 and 13.1). When interleaveDepthMs is positive, choose it so that the actual elapsed send span from the first source or repair packet of every block to its last does not exceed the signaled value. A zero value is usable only with the ISO protection_window_size alternative of . The value is not derived from a group count, frame count, or per-symbol interval.

section.name: Repair Tracks
section.t: A source track's repair tracks are the track that each of its FEC instances names in repairTrack and the tracks that name it in source ( Section 3.2; Section 10.2); Section 6 gives their conventional names. Subscription to them follows Section 7.2, and their priorities its Section 11.

section.name: FEC Signaling for Multicast Delivery
section.t: For SSM and Any-Source Multicast (ASM) delivery there is no bidirectional signaling channel. FEC parameters reach multicast receivers via:

li.t: MoQ Catalog Extension (authoritative for MoQ receivers, Section 10): out-of-band delivery in the catalog fec field (see the worked catalog of Appendix A).

MMTP AL-FEC Signaling (message_id=0x0203): in-band delivery of the AL-FEC message of Clause C.6, with Table C.3 as replaced by , for ISO/IEC 23008-1 receivers that consume the flow without the catalog, such as native broadcast (ATSC 3.0, ARIB STD-B60) receivers. A publisher that sends this message MUST carry it in an MMTP signaling packet (packet type 0x02) on packet_id 0, the MMTP signaling flow, after the signaling message payload header of Clause 9.3.4.2 (Section 3.1); on multicast delivery it shares the multicast group of the media it describes, and on MoQ delivery it MAY be carried as an object of an mmtp source track under the rules of Section 8. No track is advertised on packet_id 0 ( Section 4.1), and a receiver does not deliver these packets to a media or repair decoder (Section 3.1; Section 5)

section.t: Each FEC source flow has one FEC encoded flow ( Clause C.6.3), so the message describes a source track's flow as one entry of the message's fec_flow_descriptor naming exactly one repair flow, the track's layer-0 repair track ( Section 7.3). For a track whose instance's blockProfile is "iso-ssbg1-v1", that entry carries:

ul.li: a number_of_assets of 1, the one Asset it lists being the source track's, the Asset whose packet_id is the track's: an FEC source flow of may carry the packets of several Assets (its Clause C.1), where an FEC instance of protects one source track (its Section 5.1);

as its fec_code_id_for_repair_flow, the code point that Table 1 assigns to the code that the instance's scheme names ( Section 3): 3, the "6330 code" (RaptorQ), for "raptorq", and 1, the Reed-Solomon code, for "reed-solomon";

as its repair_flow_id, the packet_id of the layer-0 repair packets. makes this field 16 bits in the one-stage branch, where the 2023 edition of Table C.3 gives it 8 bits and so cannot name a repair packet_id above 255;

as its length_of_repair_symbol, the instance's symbolSize (T), the byte length of every repair symbol and, under ssbg_mode1, of every source symbol ( Section 10.1; and ), and as its num_of_repair_symbol_per_packet 1, the one repair symbol each repair packet carries (; Section 7.5), a field whose semantics Clause C.6.3 gives for ssbg_mode2 alone;
as its maximum_k_for_repair_flow, the instance's sourceSymbols: like that field, it bounds each block's SSB_length and is not the size of any particular block ( Section 5.4); and

as its maximum_p_for_repair_flow, the RSB_length that every repair packet of the track's FEC instance carries: the total repair count over the published layers, which is the instance's repairSymbols while layer 0 is the only published layer ( Section 7.3.1). A publisher that appends a layer ( Section 7.3.2) raises that total and sends a new version of the message carrying it only after the last repair packet generated under the previous total, of whichever block: a block's RSB_length is the total in force when its repair symbols were generated ( Section 7.5), so every repair packet sent after the new version carries a value no lower than the field it names. The path keeps no order between the message, on packet_id 0, and the repair flow (Section 5.2.2), so a receiver of both can take a packet generated under the previous total after the new version; the blocks generated under the raised total follow every block generated under the previous one in the serial order of their SS_Start ( Section 7.6), as its Section 7.3.2 requires of the publisher, which the conversion rule of Section 13.2 relies on instead.

section.t: A receiver that holds layer 0 under the AL-FEC message alone, without the catalog (), applies the fail-closed check of Section 7.3.2 with maximum_p_for_repair_flow standing for its O_0 + P_0, by that check's anchored clause alone: layer 0 has no clause of its own track, its O_0 being 0 and its symbols' coordinates depending on no published count, so a packet of the flow generated under a previous total, which the message can precede (above), fails it closed on nothing.

Layered repair is an extension of that an ISO AL-FEC message cannot express: each FEC source flow has one FEC encoded flow, whose one-stage coding structure carries a single repair_flow_id ( Clause C.6.3), so only layer 0 maps to an ISO repair flow. A repair layer is also unrelated to the layers of ISO layer-aware FEC (LA-FEC, Clause C.2.3). A publisher MUST NOT describe a repair layer above layer 0, or a keyframe overlay, in the message, whether in that entry or in an entry of its own: the one-stage coding structure names one repair flow per FEC encoded flow, the overlay protects a RAP subset that no packet_id identifies, and only the catalog declares either ( Section 7.3; and ).

section.name: Multicast Integration
section.t: MMT content can be delivered via IP multicast (SSM, AMT) and TreeDN . Platform-specific delivery paths, the multicast endpoint catalog extension, and TreeDN/AMT integration are defined in , and the multicast packet format in its Section 5.

section.name: ATSC 3.0 Compatibility
section.t: This specification is designed for interoperability with the Application-Layer FEC of ATSC A/331 MMTP sessions. applies AL-FEC to an MMTP session, when it applies it at all, through the AL-FEC framework of Annex C and requires no FEC code of its own (its Section 8.1.2.5): the framework carries whichever code the AL-FEC message names by its code point. The codes are those of , which specifies two, "reed-solomon" (code point 1, mandatory to implement) and "raptorq" (code point 3, OPTIONAL) (its Sections 3 and 10); Section 8.3 gives the AL-FEC message a publisher sends for a track of either, and an MMTP session whose AL-FEC message names any other code is outside this document and its companions until the "MoQ FEC Schemes" registry of Section 15.2 lists that code. A publisher that ingests an A/331 MMTP session takes the FEC parameters of its tracks from that message and the asset locations of the MP table (Section 13.2), and a receiver that consumes the session without the catalog takes them from the message alone, holding the one repair flow as layer 0 under the block total the message bounds, as Section 8.3 specifies. An MMTP session carries no OTI: the derived OTI of Section 6.1 fixes N = 1, and sub-blocks are never used (). ROUTE delivery, whose repair protocol (Annex A.4 of ) is RaptorQ-based, is outside the scope of this document.

section.name: ARIB STD-B60 Compatibility
section.t: ARIB STD-B60 (Japan's MMT-based broadcasting standard) uses the same ISO 23008-1 foundation as ATSC 3.0. Publishers SHOULD preserve the original FEC parameters when ingesting ARIB STD-B60 content.

section.name: Clock Reference
section.t: ARIB STD-B60 uses the MMTP Timestamp of Section 3.1: the UTC send time of the packet in NTP short format.

section.name: Transport Hierarchy
section.t: Clients SHOULD attempt transports in the preference order that Section 3 defines for native and browser clients. AL-FEC (Section 7) is the loss recovery on SSM/AMT paths, which have no retransmission.

section.name: Catalog Signaling
section.t: The MoQ catalog indicates MMT packaging and multicast endpoints.

The catalog of this suite is an MSF catalog: the root object and its fields (version, generatedAt, tracks, ...), the requirement that parsers ignore fields they do not understand, and the base per-track fields are those of Section 5. The catalog is delivered as a MoQ track whose case-sensitive Track Name is catalog ( Section 5). The documents of this suite extend the base in the same manner as extends it: this document adds the packaging value mmtp and the mmtp track fields (Section 13.1), adds the per-track fec array of FEC instances and the fec-repair and fec-source packaging values (its Sections 3 and 3.3), and adds the root-level multicast member. Every catalog field this suite uses is defined either by or locally by a document of this suite (with cmaf tracks per ); no field is defined by any other catalog specification.

A converter's output catalog is subject to the normative catalog requirements of Section 13.1 like any other catalog. A converter that adds an AMT network source advertises "driad" discovery only for a source address whose reverse DNS zone carries an AMT relay record, and otherwise names a relay service hostname in relay with "dns" discovery ( Section 4.2.1).

timescale, the group-duration field and mmtpMode are required fields (Section 13.1). The converter takes timescale from asset_timescale in the MP table when asset_timescale_flag is 1, and uses 90 000 Hz when that flag is 0, as specified by Clause 10.3.9.3. For each timed Asset, it obtains the presentation time of each MPU's first AU in presentation order from the PI document when PI is present; ISO/IEC 23008-1 Clause 10.5.2.1 says that the MPU timestamp descriptor is ignored in that case. Otherwise it decodes each descriptor's 64-bit NTP mpu_presentation_time value ( Clause 10.5.2) and does not treat the encoded NTP integer as a media tick count. It converts those presentation instants through the selected asset/media clock, retaining the authored media timing when NTP fractional quantization does not land on an integer media tick. That instant is not ticks (Section 4.4.1) when the MPU has leading pictures: ticks is that instant plus the difference between the authored composition times (Section 5.1) of the MPU's first AU in decode order and its earliest-presented AU, converted to the selected timescale as Section 4.4.1 requires.

The converter derives the group duration from the authored MPU/media cadence and validates it against those ticks values. It may emit groupDurationMs only when the conversion to the selected timescale is an exact positive integer tick count; when the cadence is exact only in ticks it emits groupDurationTicks. The fixed-cadence profile cannot represent a source whose MPU cadence is not one constant positive duration, so conversion fails rather than rounding or inventing a cadence. It sets mmtpMode itself. The AL-FEC message does not name blockProfile, which is required on every FEC instance ( Section 10.1); the converter sets it to "iso-ssbg1-v1", the profile whose entry carries the coding byte 0x14 that the converter accepts (Section 8.3; ).

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: MMT content protection uses Common Encryption (CENC) which is preserved through MoQ transport. The MMTP packet and payload headers are not encrypted by CENC, so receivers, and MMTP gateways outside MoQ, can inspect packet type, sequence, and fragmentation metadata without accessing media sample content. A MoQ relay treats the object payload, MMTP headers included, as opaque ( Section 7.8) and never parses MMTP (Section 6.2).

section.name: ATSC 3.0 Signed Region (A3SA)
section.t: Per Section 5.2.2.5, the ATSC 3.0 signing mechanism, whose certificates the ATSC 3.0 Security Authority (A3SA) administers, covers signaling messages and MA3 messages (packet type 0x2) but excludes asset packets (type 0x00 MPU and type 0x03 repair).

Neither nor carries the SS_ID inside the A3SA signed region. In particular the MMT hint sample does not: neither its ISO syntax ( Clause 8.3.2) nor the ATSC MMTHSampleATSC3 syntax ( Section 7.2.4.2.2.3) has a Source FEC Payload ID field, and hint samples travel as MPU-mode data units on the Asset's own packet_id ( Section 7.2.4.2.3), that is in asset packets, which A3SA does not sign. This document therefore defines no A3SA-authenticated FEC block assignment: block assignment taken from the trailing Source FEC Payload ID () of an A3SA verified packet is unauthenticated. A receiver that requires authenticated FEC block assignment MUST obtain it from an integrity mechanism, other than A3SA signing, whose coverage includes the complete MMTP packet, the trailer included. Version 2 of the bc-provenance profile ( Section 7.2) is such a mechanism: its digest covers the whole UDP payload as transmitted, the Source FEC Payload ID included. The same holds for the overlay SS_ID (): A3SA signing authenticates neither, and a receiver that requires authenticated block assignment treats each as this section requires.

An attacker who can modify the Source FEC Payload ID without detection could redirect source symbols to incorrect FEC blocks, causing recovery failures or corrupted output. On multicast networks without A3SA verification, receivers SHOULD cross-check the SS_ID against the MMTP packet_sequence_number to detect obvious tampering (e.g., an SS_ID that advances further than the packet_sequence_number of the same packet_id, whereas SS_ID advances by one per FEC source packet, ).

section.name: Multicast Security
section.t: Multicast-specific security considerations (source authentication, replay protection, AMT relay trust) are defined in Section 7.

section.t: This document defines the catalog packaging value "mmtp" (Section 13.1), extending the allowed packaging values of the MOQT Streaming Format Section 5.2.4 in the same manner as . If a registry of packaging values is established for that format, this document requests registration of:

The header extension type 0x8B01 of is an MMTP value, not a MoQ one; Clause 9.2.3 defines no registry of MMTP header extension types, so its use requires no IANA action.

Sentences that are new rather than moved, listed verbatim with the -01 text they replace where one exists:

This specification defines the mapping of MMT packets to MoQ objects, the "iso-ssbg1-v1" block profile under which the Forward Error Correction (FEC) mechanism for MoQ protects MMTP packets -- its source symbols, its Source FEC Payload ID trailer, its repair packet and its keyframe overlay -- the derivation of MoQ catalogs from MMTP signaling, and compatibility considerations for both ATSC 3.0 and ARIB STD-B60 systems, including the ATSC 3.0 signed region.
FEC: MMT's AL-FEC integrates with MoQ FEC repair tracks per [MOQ-FEC-CORE], under the "iso-ssbg1-v1" block profile that this document defines (Section 7)
Broadcast interworking: ATSC 3.0 A/331 AL-FEC sessions and the ATSC 3.0 signed region (Sections 10 and 14.1), and ARIB STD-B60 (Section 11)
The last column names the block profile under which the FEC mechanism of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] protects tracks of each packaging.
"moq-object-v1" is the profile of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.2: each loc or cmaf object whose Object Status is Normal occupies whole source symbols.
"iso-ssbg1-v1" is the profile that Section 7.1 of this document defines: each FEC source packet (FEC Type 1) is one source symbol.
Both are registered in the "MoQ FEC Block Profiles" registry of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 15.3.

A publisher that offers CMAF content can also carry it as an mmtp track under "iso-ssbg1-v1", where an MPU corresponds to a CMAF Fragment (Section 4.2). [reworded from -01 13 3893-3895: "Alternatively, the publisher carries the media as an mmtp track under iso-ssbg1-v1, where an MPU corresponds to a CMAF Fragment (see [MOQ-MMT])"; the alternative it followed, direct protection under "moq-object-v1", is [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 13.2, and the pointer to this document became a pointer to Section 4.2; the two sentences that follow are carried verbatim from -01 13 3895-3900 with the Section 4.1 citation written as a token]

Section 1.2, all four sentences: This document is a companion of [MOQ-FEC-CORE], which defines the scheme-independent FEC mechanism for MoQ and the configuration data model that a catalog carries. [MOQ-FEC-BLOCK] specifies the Reed-Solomon and RaptorQ schemes, [MOQ-FEC-CATALOG] the catalog encoding of the configuration, and [MOQ-FEC-MULTICAST] the delivery of protected tracks over multicast, including the receiver repair policy. This document defines the "iso-ssbg1-v1" block profile, the part of that set that is specific to MMTP packets, and the ATSC 3.0 and ARIB STD-B60 interworking that relies on it. [MOQ-MULTICAST] defines multicast endpoint discovery and the multicast packet format on which the multicast delivery of mmtp tracks rests.

The FEC terms of this document -- Source Track, Repair Track, Repair Layer, FEC Instance, Source Symbol, Repair Symbol, Source Block, SS_ID, SS_Start, SSB_length, RS_ID, RSB_length, Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) and Block Profile -- are those of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 2, and the RS_ID offset O_i and per-block repair symbol count P_i of layer i are those of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 7.3.1.
Under "iso-ssbg1-v1" the following take a form of their own, and the remaining terms are specific to this document:

Base Instance: Of a source track that a keyframe overlay protects, the instance that is not the overlay; of any other source track, its only instance. (New definition; -01 used the term without defining it. [MOQ-FEC-MULTICAST] Section 2 carries the same text.)

[MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.6 requires every source object to carry the FEC Source Info Object Property (type 0x11); on an mmtp source object its value is the four-byte form of that section, which names instance 0 and carries the network-byte-order SS_ID of the base instance, the value of the packet's Source FEC Payload ID (Section 7.2); the property is object metadata and is not inserted into this payload.

A subscriber finds the repair tracks of the rendition it selects through the repairTrack of each of that rendition's FEC instances and the source fields of its repair tracks ([MOQ-FEC-CATALOG] Section 3.2; the data model of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 10.2).
This section defines that profile, "iso-ssbg1-v1": its source symbols, the Source FEC Payload ID trailer, the MMTP form of the repair packet, the keyframe overlay and the interleave window.
It states where the profile deviates from [MOQ-FEC-CORE], whose remaining rules apply unchanged ([MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.2).
The rules of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] apply to a track under this profile with the following deviations, which [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.2 asks a companion profile to state:

The unit of protection is the MMTP packet, not the MoQ object: a source symbol is formed from one FEC source packet as this section specifies, and the Protected Object Unit of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.2 is not used.
A source object of an mmtp track carries one source symbol, the FEC source packet that is its payload, so SS_IDs advance by one per source object.
A source packet carries its SS_ID in a 4-byte trailer, the Source FEC Payload ID (Section 7.2), which is the canonical carrier.

The FEC Source Info Object Property of the object that carries the packet restates it in the 4-byte form, which names instance 0 ([MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.6); the Property is object metadata, not part of the protected packet, and is not recovered with it.

When an object carries a source symbol but no FEC Source Info Property, a receiver that parses the packet MAY take the SS_ID from the trailer and feed the symbol to the base decoder (Section 7.2), a deviation from [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.6, under which such an object is not a source object; a receiver that does not parse the packet has no SS_ID for it and feeds it to no decoder. [new; restates the -01 5.3 permission (1103-1104) as a deviation in the Section 7.1 list]
A repair object is one complete MMTP repair packet of 12 + 13 + T bytes (Section 7.3), not the 13 + T byte payload of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 7.5.

The keyframe overlay (Section 7.4) is this profile's form of an overlapping instance ([MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 8.4), with two differences from that section and from [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 5.1: a RAP packet's overlay SS_ID travels in an MMTP header extension, not in a second entry of the FEC Source Info Property, and the Property keeps the 4-byte form, so a receiver learns a packet's overlay membership and overlay SS_ID from that extension, which lies inside the protected packet (Section 7.4.2), rather than from the Property alone; and because a recovered packet carries its overlay SS_ID but not its base SS_ID, a base recovery places the packet in the overlay instance, whereas an overlay recovery counts toward the base instance only where the receiver has determined the packet's base SS_ID independently (Section 7.1). [the clauses from "with two differences" on are new, restating Sections 7.1, 7.2 and 7.4.2 against the core's instance-membership rule]

The symbol carriage of [MOQ-FEC-CORE] Section 6.2, and with it the symbol track and the FEC Unit Start Property, does not apply to an mmtp track: its source symbols reach a receiver inside the track's own objects or as multicast datagrams ([MOQ-MULTICAST] Section 5), each carrying one whole FEC source packet.

This profile uses ssbg_mode1, with the one-stage FEC coding structure and FEC payload ID mode 0 ([ISO.23008-1] Clause C.1). a track under "moq-object-v1" has no overlay, and a catalog that declares one for such a track fails the rule of Section 7.4.1. [-01 7.6.6 2629-2634 condensed]

section.name: MMTP Symbol Capacity Example
section.t: This appendix is informative. It carries the MMTP capacity arithmetic of the catalog example of draft-ramadan-moq-fec-01 (), Appendix B of that revision, as a historical example: its parameters are the ones shown here, and are not those of the worked catalog of .
section.artwork: video: scheme raptorq, K 625, P 125, T 1000, groupDurationMs 1000, interleaveDepthMs 1000, bitrate 4990000 bit/s audio: scheme raptorq, K 32, P 8, T 512, groupDurationMs 1000, interleaveDepthMs 1000, bitrate 128000 bit/s
section.t: The video instance is valid only under "raptorq", since 625 + 125 = 750 exceeds the "reed-solomon" bound of 255 ( Section 7); the audio instance, with 32 + 8 = 40, is within that bound under either scheme.

Parameter consistency: both tracks use one-second MMTP groups (one MPU per MoQ Group), and each has a 1000 ms source/repair send-span budget. The group duration does not determine the FEC partition. A worked capacity check must include the MMTP and MPU-mode headers, not only the media bitrate. With no MMTP header extension, a timed FT=2 packet has the following media capacity, depending on whether it starts a data unit (Section 5.2):
section.artwork: FI=0 or FI=1: T - 2 (length) - 12 (MMTP) - 8 (MPU) - 14 (DU) = T - 36 FI=2 or FI=3: T - 2 (length) - 12 (MMTP) - 8 (MPU) = T - 22
section.t: The source packet also carries a 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID on the wire, outside the protected packet and therefore outside these symbol budgets (). FT=0/FT=1 metadata consumes source packets but does not carry sample bytes, and any MMTP extension consumes additional space. Every protected MMTP packet still must fit within T - 2 (). Using the larger continuation capacity gives a media ceiling, not a packetization plan:

li.t: Video: 4,990,000 bit/s x 1.0 s / 8 = 623,750 bytes of media per one-second group. K x (T - 22) = 625 x 978 = 611,250 bytes is an upper bound on the media capacity of one full block. The media therefore needs at least ceil(623,750 / 978) = 638 source packets and at least two K=625 blocks; MMTP metadata, fragmentation, and authored packet boundaries can require more. Repair overhead is P / K = 125 / 625 = 20%.

section.t: The publisher must choose the actual source-packet count and block boundaries so that every packet, including FT=0 and FT=1 metadata, fits the selected symbol size and every block's repair fields describe the actual (SS_Start, SSB_length) partition. These calculations are capacity examples, not a rule that one FEC block equals one Group.
